citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care.
citations.narrative:
A veterinarian had prescribed 3 doses of Meloxicam (1 dose every 24 hours) to a macaque that had undergone a bone
marrow aspirate on February 3, 2026. The macaque received the first dose of Meloxicam along with local anesthetic, and
an opioid. The subsequent two doses of meloxicam were entered into the system to be given the following two days by
veterinary staff. The veterinary technician believed the drugs were being given by another group and did not give the
second dose. On day 3, the error was noted and the final dose was given as prescribed. Miscommunication was the
cause of the second dose not being given, as prescribed.
Two dogs did not receive a dose of Carprofen after a histotripsy procedure on 5/6/2026. The animals received the first
dose of Carprofen after the procedure with other drugs, but a documentation error prevented the dogs from getting the
second dose the next day.
A macaque underwent repair surgery to remove granulation tissue and existing bone regrowth within a cranial chamber
and was prescribed analgesics post procedure. Simbadol was one of the prescribed drugs, and the animal did not receive
the dose that was prescribed. Staff transition and miscommunication were the cause for this error.
Each research facility shall establish and maintain programs of veterinary care that include adequate pre-procedural and
post-procedural care in accordance with current established medical procedures.
Corrected prior to inspection on 21 May 2026.

A macaque underwent surgery and was returned to its enclosure on January 7,2026. To limit activity in the immediate
post-operative period, the enclosure was partially closed. The husbandry team placed food in one half of the enclosure for
the animal after recovery. However, the surgery team returned the animal to the other side of the enclosure and failed to
notice the lack of food on that half. The animal was immediately provided with food the next morning upon discovery.
Failure to provide sufficient quality and quantity of food can negatively impact on the health and well-being of the animals.
Non-human primates must be fed at least once each day except as otherwise might be required to provide adequate
veterinary care.
Corrected prior to inspection on 21 May 2026.

A macaque had been fasted for sedation and clinical treatment at 8 AM on February 17, 2026. After the exam, the animal
was placed back into a restricted pen to recover before returning to the group pen. At approximately 3:15pm, the animal
was checked by husbandry staff and was noted to not be fully recovered from sedation, so it was left separated from the
group to continue recovery. The husbandry technician planned to recheck the animal later that afternoon but
subsequently forgot. The next morning a technician found that the animal was mistakenly placed on the side of the pen
that did not have water and food. Lack of potable water in sufficient quantity to nonhuman primates can negatively impact
their health and well-being.
Potable water must be provided in sufficient quantity to every nonhuman primate housed at the facility.
Corrected prior to inspection on 21 May 2026.

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
A husbandry manager determined that beginning in August 2025 and for several additional months, the cage sanitation
for one Nonhuman Primate vivarium exceeded the required 14-day interval. Cage sanitation was delayed 48-72 hours,
and on one occasion, was delayed 6 days. However, daily cleaning of the cages continued. Multiple animal health
technicians were involved in the cage sanitation delay, due to instructions by a facility supervisor. Sanitation is a critical
step to avoid cross contamination and prevent potential transmission of diseases to the macaques.
Primary enclosures must be sanitized at least once every 2 weeks either using live stream under pressure or with hot
water (at least 180 °F) and as often as necessary to prevent the growth of microorganisms that could potentially cause
disease in non-human primates.
Corrected prior to inspection on 21 May 2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the facility representatives.
